sections.overview: The giant panda is a bear of central China, now confined to scattered mountain forests in Sichuan, Shaanxi and Gansu. Its diet is almost entirely bamboo, although its body remains recognizably that of a bear rather than a specialized grazing mammal. Adults usually forage alone, but overlapping ranges and scent trails help them find one another during the breeding season.
sections.identification: The panda has a broad head, sturdy body and dense woolly coat: black fur marks its ears, eye patches, shoulders and legs, while its face and trunk are white. Adults are about 1.2 to 1.8 metres long; wild males can reach 113 kilograms and females rarely reach 104 kilograms, figures near the upper end rather than typical weights. Strong jaw muscles and broad molars crush tough bamboo stems. Beside five ordinary digits, each forepaw has an enlarged radial sesamoid, a small wrist bone covered by a fleshy pad. This so-called pseudo-thumb is relatively immobile: the five fingers flex around a bamboo stalk against it, while the panda’s teeth tear the stalk. The bone acts as a passive stop, not an active pinching finger, and its form balances feeding grip with bearing weight when the paw meets the ground.
sections.habitat: Wild pandas survive in six mountain systems across Sichuan, Shaanxi and Gansu, in moist broadleaf or conifer forests with bamboo beneath the canopy. These forests usually lie around 1,500 to 3,000 metres above sea level, often under heavy rain or mist. In one Foping study in the Qinling Mountains, six GPS-collared pandas shifted between lower and higher ranges as different bamboo shoots and leaves came into season. That local pattern shows how a home range can include several feeding zones rather than one bamboo patch. Farming, timber extraction and forest clearing have removed lowland habitat, while broken forest can obstruct travel and contact between populations.
sections.diet: Bamboo is the panda’s staple food, and a wild adult may spend about 12 hours a day feeding. Across the year it selects tender shoots, leaves and stems as their availability changes. Its short digestive tract resembles that of other bears and extracts little energy from bamboo; it ferments plant fibre only to a limited degree. Captive feeding trials found low energy digestibility on bamboo-only diets, so much of the food’s energy remains unavailable to the animal. Field estimates put daily intake at roughly 13 to 15 kilograms of leaves and stems, while intake of watery shoots can be much higher. A study of eight pandas—five captive and three wild—measured daily energy expenditure at 37.7 percent of the amount predicted for a mammal of similar size, consistent with a low-activity lifestyle that reduces energy needs.
sections.behavior: Pandas are mostly solitary, yet overlapping ranges, scent stations and occasional meetings create a loose social network. Glands near the anus leave chemical marks on trees, rocks and paths; these can carry information about sex, individual identity and reproductive condition. During the short breeding season, pandas also call as they approach through dense bamboo. In playback trials, females distinguished individual males’ bleats, evidence that calls can help coordinate close encounters. At other times, scent marks often help animals avoid one another. Feeding alternates with rests of several hours; pandas also climb and swim, though most of their active time is spent on the ground.
sections.reproduction: Females come into heat once each spring, often for only two or three days, so mating is concentrated in a brief window. After fertilization, the embryo can pause before attaching to the uterus, a process called delayed implantation that shifts the timing of birth. Field observations in the Qinling Mountains recorded most matings in March and April; pregnancy lasted four to five months overall, including about one and a half to two months after implantation. The same study recorded births from mid-August to early September. Captive records put newborns at about 90 to 130 grams: pink, nearly hairless and blind, they are tiny beside their mother. She nurses the helpless cub in a sheltered den. Zoo observations report that cubs open their eyes at six to eight weeks. In the Qinling field study, young pandas left the den at about three to four months. Litters can include twins. Milk remains important through infancy; captive records show nursing for eight to nine months and social separation may occur later.
sections.ecology: Pandas depend on bamboo, whose shoots and leaves change in quality and availability through the year. At Wolong, the preferred bamboo Bashania fangiana mass-flowered and died in 1983, sharply reducing the standing crop. Pandas changed what they ate and, two years later, began using more of a lower-elevation alternative bamboo, Fargesia robusta. In the Qinling Mountains, seasonal shifts between bamboo species were documented among tracked pandas in Foping. A separate Qinling study found seasonal dietary overlap between pandas and wild boar eating shoots, suggesting potential competition for a brief, nutritious food. Connected forest can help pandas reach alternate feeding areas as bamboo resources shift.
sections.conservation: Hunting for pelts, farming, timber extraction and settlement reduced the panda’s range and broke mountain forests into isolated patches. China’s fourth national survey, conducted in 2011–2014 and published in 2015, reported 1,864 wild pandas at the end of 2013 and 67 reserves in the range, while noting fragmentation and small populations at risk. A 2021 analysis of those census data found that 25 of 33 populations held about 259 pandas, around 14 percent of the wild total. In 2016 the IUCN changed the species’ Red List category from Endangered to Vulnerable after population growth linked to forest protection and restoration, while recognizing continuing risks. Reserves, forest restoration and corridors aim to reconnect habitat, but isolated groups remain vulnerable to habitat loss and limited exchange.
